issues.legal_issue: A statutory process permitting arrest and detention to recover public tax dues is constitutionally valid when it includes safeguards against arbitrary detention.
material_facts: Tax dues were recoverable as public arrears, and the recovery law authorized arrest and detention as one means of collection.
The law limited the duration of detention and exempted specified categories of persons from arrest and detention.

The rules required the arrested defaulter to be brought promptly before the issuing officer and prohibited detention unless the officer had reason to believe it would compel payment of the whole or a substantial part of the arrears.
The court considered arrest and detention a coercive means of recovering public dues, not punishment for mere default.
issues.conclusion: The statutory recovery process was not violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(d), or 21 of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: A restriction on freedom of movement must not be arbitrary or excessive; its reasonableness is assessed by balancing individual freedom against the public interest in light of the circumstances. Coercive recovery of public dues may be reasonable when adequate safeguards govern detention. The court applied State of Madras v. V.G. Row, The Collector of Malabar v. Erimal Ebrahim Hajee, and Sangam Lal Gupta v. Sales Tax Officer, and followed Purshottam Govindji Halai on a State's ability to devise machinery for recovering its public demands.

rule.if: public_dues_recovery_proceeding and arrest_and_detention_are_authorized and detention_is_time_limited and protected_persons_are_exempt and detention_requires_a_productivity_finding

predicates.public_dues_recovery_proceeding: An authority is seeking to recover dues owed to the government as public arrears.
predicates.arrest_and_detention_are_authorized: The recovery process permits arrest and detention as a means of collecting the arrears.
predicates.detention_is_time_limited: The governing process limits how long a defaulter may be detained.
predicates.protected_persons_are_exempt: The governing process exempts specified categories of persons from arrest or detention.
predicates.detention_requires_a_productivity_findin: The officer must determine that detention is likely to compel payment of the whole or a substantial part of the arrears before ordering detention.

issues.definition: When public dues are pursued through authorized arrest and detention subject to a time limit, exemptions, and a required finding that detention can compel payment, the recovery process is not unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: The international prohibition on imprisonment merely for inability to fulfil a contractual obligation does not bar arrest in a statutory recovery proceeding for public tax dues.
material_facts: The dues were tax liabilities imposed by statute, not debts arising from a contractual obligation.
The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights had not been made part of Indian municipal law.
The petitioners relied on the Covenant's prohibition on imprisonment merely for inability to fulfil a contractual obligation.
issues.conclusion: Article 11 of the Covenant did not aid the petitioners in challenging arrest for recovery of the statutory public dues.
issues.legal_principle: Article 11 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights had not been incorporated into Indian municipal law and concerns a debt due under a contractual obligation. Jolly George Verghese v. Bank of Cochin was distinguished because it concerned execution under section 51 of the Code of Civil Procedure and a contractual debt.

predicates.public_tax_recovery_proceeding: An authority is seeking to recover tax imposed by law as a public due.
predicates.obligation_is_statutory_public_debt: The payment obligation arises under a statute rather than a contract.
predicates.covenant_not_part_of_municipal_law: The international covenant relied on has not been made part of the domestic legal system.

issues.definition: When a statutory public tax debt is being recovered and the covenant is not part of domestic law, the covenant does not bar arrest for that recovery.

issues.legal_issue: The arrest-and-detention procedure expressly governed by a special public-revenue recovery scheme is not governed in terms by the civil procedure rules for arrest in execution of a decree.
material_facts: The tax recovery law permitted collection as arrears of land revenue and also gave the Collector civil-court powers for recovery of an amount due under a decree.
The special revenue statute and its rules expressly set out the procedure for arrest and detention.

The general civil-procedure provisions applied to proceedings under the special statute only unless otherwise expressly provided, and the statute expressly referred to civil-procedure rules for certain other recovery methods but not arrest and detention.
issues.conclusion: Section 51 of the Code of Civil Procedure did not apply in terms to arrest and detention under the special revenue recovery scheme.
issues.legal_principle: Where a special statute and rules provide a complete procedure for arrest and detention, the general application of the Code of Civil Procedure does not displace that procedure. The court relied on the relevant provisions of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, and its Rules, and held that Seth Banarsi Das Gupta v. State of U.P. did not correctly state the law on section 51 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.public_dues_recovery_proceeding: An authority is using a statutory process to recover public dues.
predicates.arrest_process_is_expressly_governed_by_: A special recovery scheme expressly sets out how arrest and detention are to be carried out.
predicates.general_civil_procedure_applies_only_whe: The governing law makes general civil procedure applicable only where the special scheme does not expressly provide otherwise.
predicates.special_scheme_does_not_adopt_civil_arre: The special scheme does not expressly incorporate the general civil procedure for arrest in execution of a decree.

issues.definition: When public-dues arrest is expressly governed by a special scheme that does not adopt the civil arrest procedure, that general procedure does not apply in terms.

issues.legal_issue: A defaulter ordinarily must receive prior notice of the recovery demand before the drastic process of arrest is used.
material_facts: The revenue rules contemplated that a demand or citation ordinarily issue before another recovery process is used.

The court held that, even without a formal demand, the nature of the arrest process implies that the defaulter should have prior notice that a recovery certificate has issued so payment can be made to avoid arrest.
issues.conclusion: A writ of demand or citation should ordinarily be issued before an arrest warrant; if no formal writ is issued, prior notice of the recovery certificate is implicit in the process.
issues.legal_principle: The ordinary sequence of recovery processes requires a demand or citation before resort to arrest. The court relied on the rule governing ordinary issuance of a demand or citation and on the implicit requirement of prior notice inherent in the arrest process.

predicates.public_dues_recovery_proceeding: An authority is pursuing a statutory process to recover public dues.
predicates.arrest_is_being_considered_as_a_recovery: The authority is considering arrest as a means of collecting the arrears.

issues.definition: When arrest is being considered to recover public dues, the defaulter ordinarily must first receive notice of the recovery demand.

issues.legal_issue: An arrest warrant cannot support detention when the required inquiry into whether detention would compel payment has not been conducted.
material_facts: Arrest warrants had been issued against some defaulters in the course of tax recovery proceedings.
The officer who issued the warrant had not conducted the required inquiry into whether detention would compel payment of the arrears or a substantial portion of them.
The governing rule required that inquiry before detention and required release if the officer was not satisfied that detention would be productive of payment.
issues.conclusion: The existing warrants were quashed and could not be used to detain the petitioners, without prejudice to the authorities' ability to make fresh orders in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: The rule governing detention after arrest requires the issuing officer to inquire whether detention will compel payment of the whole or a substantial portion of the arrears and permits detention only upon the requisite satisfaction. The court applied Rule 251 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Rules.

predicates.public_tax_recovery_arrest_proceeding: An authority is pursuing arrest as part of a proceeding to recover public tax arrears.
predicates.arrest_warrant_has_been_issued: An officer has issued a warrant to arrest the defaulter.
predicates.required_detention_productivity_inquiry_: The officer did not inquire whether detention would compel payment of the whole or a substantial part of the arrears.

issues.definition: When a public-tax recovery arrest warrant has issued without the required inquiry into whether detention can compel payment, the warrant cannot support detention and must be quashed.
